name: Saint-Malo
title: Saint-Malo Ship Gauging | UTM at the Rance Estuary Port
description: Thickness measurement at Saint-Malo for ferries to Portsmouth and the Channel Islands, cargo ships and fishing vessels: tidal locks, decks, tanks and piping.
h1: UTM and Hull Gauging for Ships at Saint-Malo
intro: Saint-Malo is a tidal port on the Rance estuary with one of the largest tidal ranges in Europe, so ships work to the water as much as to the schedule. Ferries to Portsmouth and the Channel Islands, cargo ships, fishing boats and yachts all use it. Superintendents gauge ferries between sailings and cargo ships on the commercial quay, with technicians mobilised from India to meet the ship at the berth.

highlights.h: Tide-led timing at a lock port
highlights.p: Saint-Malo's tidal range sets when ships can enter and leave the inner basins. The gauging plan follows the lock times and the water, and starts with the spaces the superintendent needs first.

highlights.h: Ferries to England and the Channel Islands
highlights.p: Ro-pax and fast ferries link the port to Portsmouth, Jersey and Guernsey. Layovers between sailings and seasonal lay-up give windows for deck, tank and piping gauging.
Trawlers, coastal fishing vessels and small cargo ships lie in the commercial and fishing basins. Hull and tank readings are fitted around landings and the tide on those berths.

port.h: Saint-Malo: a walled city and a tidal harbour
p: Saint-Malo stands at the mouth of the Rance on the northern coast of Brittany, behind a ring of islets and reefs that make the approach to the harbour a matter for pilots. The tidal range here is among the largest in Europe, so the water in the outer harbour rises and falls by many metres twice a day. The port's inner basins are shut off by locks to keep ships afloat at low water, and commercial ships enter and leave on the tide. The old walled city that gives the port its name overlooks the entrance, and the ferry terminal and commercial quays lie to the south of it.

The traffic splits into passenger, cargo and fishing. Ferries run from the terminal to Portsmouth, on the English south coast, and to Jersey and Guernsey in the Channel Islands, using ro-pax and, in summer, fast craft. The commercial quays handle bulk and general cargo on short-sea ships, including fertiliser, timber, animal fodder and construction materials for Brittany and Normandy. A fishing fleet and a large number of yachts and sail-training vessels use the basins, and cruise ships anchor off the walls on summer calls, with passengers landed by tender.

The tide shapes everything for inspection. A cargo ship arrives on the flood, locks in, discharges and leaves on the next suitable tide, so a stay of two or three tides is typical. Ferries have fixed schedules but are affected by the same water at the terminal. A ship that needs a dry dock goes elsewhere: the larger yards at Brest or Cherbourg, or a facility in the Channel Islands or England, are more suited to ships of ferry size. What Saint-Malo gives the superintendent is access at the quay and the anchorage, and readings that make the next docking shorter.

facilities.h: Where gauging can be done at Saint-Malo
p: Ferry berths at the terminal give the standard ferry windows: vehicle decks gauged when they are clear, ramp and door structure while the ship is alongside, and tanks and machinery spaces within the permit system. A seasonal ferry laid by in the off-season is a better target, because the whole ship is quiet and the larger scope of deck, tank and piping gauging can be done in a block. Scheduling follows the tide, which affects when the ship is accessible by gangway and when stores or staff can be transferred.

On the commercial quays the typical subject is a short-sea cargo ship in the basin behind the locks. Holds, coamings and hatch covers can be gauged when empty, and ballast tanks are worked in parallel. Fishing vessels lie in their own basin, and hull plating, tanks and sea-water piping are measured around their landings and the tide. Ships at anchor off the harbour are reached by launch arranged by the agent, with swell and tidal streams limiting the time on board. Because the approach is tricky and the tide strong, the gauging team is briefed by the agent before every launch.
list: Ferry terminal berths — vehicle deck, ramp, door and ballast tank gauging on ro-pax and fast ferries between sailings.
Seasonal ferry lay-by — larger deck, tank and piping scopes on ships laid by in the off-season.
Commercial quays behind the locks — hold, coaming, hatch cover and ballast tank gauging on short-sea cargo ships.
Fishing basin berths — hull plating, tank and sea-water piping readings on trawlers and coastal fishing vessels.
Outer harbour and roads anchorage — launch-served readings on ships waiting for the tide or a berth.
Repair berths for small craft — wall-thickness checks on piping and deck structure during repair afloat.

context.h: Regulation and the Channel Islands link
p: Port state control in France follows the Paris MoU, and the Centres de sécurité des navires of the French maritime administration carry out the inspections. Ferries between France, England and the Channel Islands cross several jurisdictions in a single day, and their owners need records that stand up in any of them. Thickness readings on decks, ramps and the lower hull give the superintendent a dated measurement that supports class and flag discussions, and shows where renewal is due at the next docking.

Passenger ships follow the class society's hull survey rules rather than the Enhanced Survey Programme, with the extent of gauging growing at each special survey. Small bulk carriers and tankers calling at the commercial quays fall under ESP and the IACS hull survey requirements for their type. The EU Ship Recycling Regulation requires an Inventory of Hazardous Materials on ships calling at EU ports, and EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime shape the economics of every voyage. For owners of ageing short-sea cargo ships the gauging is often part of a plan to decide whether to renew steel or retire the ship.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs in Saint-Malo
jobs.p: Most requests combine a ferry or cargo schedule with the tidal timetable. The superintendent supplies the class gauging requirements and the planned stays, and we build a priority list that works even if a lock time moves or a sailing is delayed. Seasonal ferry lay-ups and cargo stays on the commercial quay offer the longest windows. Typical jobs include:
list: Vehicle deck plating, ramp and stern door gauging on a ro-pax ferry laid by for the off-season at the terminal.
Ballast tank and double-bottom readings on a ferry ahead of its refit, providing the yard with a measured steel list.
Hold frame, coaming and hatch cover gauging on a short-sea cargo ship locked into the basin to discharge fertiliser or timber.
Hull plating and sea-water piping gauging on a fishing vessel during a quiet period in the fishing basin.
Pre-purchase condition gauging for a buyer of a small coaster lying at the commercial quay.

logistics: Technicians usually fly to Paris and take the high-speed train to Rennes, then continue by rail or road to Saint-Malo, while the airport at Dinard, close to the port, has seasonal connections but is rarely the practical route from India. The ship's agent arranges access to the terminal or the commercial quay and books launches for ships at anchor. France is a Schengen state, so every technician needs a Schengen visa, applied for when the call is confirmed, with an invitation letter from the owner naming the ship. Travel plans are adjusted to the tide times the agent supplies.
vessels: Small bulk carriers and fertiliser carriers

faqs.q: How does the tidal range affect gauging at Saint-Malo?
faqs.a: It decides when ships enter the basins and when gangways, access and launches are workable. We take the lock and tide times from the ship's agent and put the most important spaces first, so that a shifted lock time or a short stay does not remove the readings the superintendent most needs.

faqs.q: Is there a dry dock at Saint-Malo for a ferry docking?
faqs.a: Ferry-sized ships normally dock at a larger yard, such as Brest or Cherbourg, or in England or the Channel Islands. What we do at Saint-Malo is the gauging in advance, so the yard has a measured steel list and the dock stay is spent on repair.

faqs.q: Can a ferry laid up for the winter be gauged in a single visit?
faqs.a: Often yes, because the ship is quiet and the whole vessel is available. Vehicle decks, ramps, tanks and piping can be measured in a block over several days, in a sequence agreed with the superintendent, giving a full steel picture before the refit.

faqs.q: Can fishing vessels be gauged in the fishing basin?
faqs.a: Yes. Trawlers and coastal fishing vessels can have hull plating, tanks and sea-water piping measured while they lie in the basin, fitted around landings and the tide. Owners often combine this with a planned docking elsewhere, where readings help to set the repair list.
